Florence, May. Pietro is back in the newsroom: the editor, Carlo Ferri, shows him how to turn a news item into a headline.
So, young man. The news is: "Yesterday the company and the family signed an agreement and the trattoria will stay open." Give me a headline.
"Yesterday the company and the family signed…"
Too long. A headline has to fit on one line. Take out "yesterday": the reader knows it was yesterday.
Better. Did you see? You used the present. In headlines the present is used for the past too. It's livelier.
Shorter still. Take out the verb "to be" and the articles. The participle is enough.
Exactly. And now add the place with a colon and the most important thing at the end.
"Via Maggio, agreement signed: the trattoria stays."
Perfect. And above it, in the kicker, we put: "After a month of tug-of-war".
Tug-of-war? But nobody did any arm-wrestling!
In the papers they do, young man. Every day. And when it ends well, it's called "white smoke". Like when they elect the Pope.
Double CC followed by i: BRAC-cio, with "cio" as in "chop".
S followed by V is voiced, like "zv": ZVOL-ta.

The day after the meeting, Pietro bought an album with a green cover and began cutting out every article that mentioned the trattoria. He glued them in order, one per page, with the date written above in capitals. Davide drew small steaming pots in the margins, cats in braces and a Ms Conti holding her glasses. By the end of May the album was half full, and it told a story nobody could have predicted at the start.

Page one, Friday 17 April. Kicker: "Packed meeting in the Oltrarno". Headline: "Via Maggio, the neighbourhood defends its trattoria". Standfirst: "Two hundred people, three hours of debate. Councillor Neri: 'We will start the application for historic shops'". Below was the photo of Pietro standing on the chair, the sheet in his hand and his mouth open. Graziella had had it framed by the framer in Via Toscanella before Pietro had even glued it into the album.

Page two, Tuesday 21 April. Headline: "Arno Living: 'The project does not change'". It was the shortest article in the album, but also the coldest. The company's board, meeting in Milan, had announced in a press release that the plan for the twelve flats "was going ahead according to schedule". There was no mention of Ms Conti. Pietro had glued the article in crooked, on purpose, and next to it Davide had drawn a black cloud.

Page three, Sunday 26 April. Kicker: "After the Via Maggio meeting". Headline: "Short-term rentals: controversy across the city". It was no longer only about the trattoria. Other neighbourhoods had organised meetings: in Santa Croce, in San Niccolò, in Sant'Ambrogio. The letters to the editor had become so many that the paper had opened a special page, "The residents have their say". Rita's letter had been the first to be published.

Page three bis, Wednesday 29 April, had been added by Pietro with a little fear. Headline: "Arno Living threatens legal action: 'The register doesn't apply to us'". According to the company's lawyers, the building had been bought before the trattoria entered the register, so the new rules could not be applied. Councillor Neri had replied with a sentence Mancini put in the next day's headline: "Rules apply to everyone, even to people who come from Milan". A real tug-of-war, the paper wrote, had begun.

That week Davide published his second cartoon. This time there were two arms, one in the sleeve of an elegant jacket and the other in the sleeve of a kitchen apron, arm-wrestling on a trattoria table. The arm with the apron was winning, but only just. In a corner, under the table, a grey and white dog with enormous ears was waiting for something to fall. When Lupino saw it hanging on the fridge, he barked twice. Graziella said that was his way of signing it.

Page four was the strangest. It wasn't an article but a small item at the bottom of the business page: "Arno Living: head of Tuscany operations resigns". Pietro hadn't noticed it. Bellini had found it, as he read the paper from the last page to the first, "because they always hide the important news at the back". When Pietro read it, he got scared. "Did she resign because of us?" he asked. Bellini said nothing. Nobody knew.

The answer came three days later, on a Wednesday evening, as the trattoria was about to close. The door opened and Ms Conti walked in. She wasn't wearing the blue suit, but a grey jumper and jeans, and under her arm she carried a different folder, old, made of cardboard. She sat at the same table as at the meeting and asked shyly if there was a plate of ribollita left. Graziella asked no questions. She brought it, then sat down opposite her and waited.

"I've resigned," said Valeria Conti when she had finished eating. "Not because of you. Thanks to you." She opened the cardboard folder. Inside was a handwritten menu, yellowed, with an oil stain in one corner: "Trattoria da Nella, Prato, 1971". "It was my grandmother's," she explained. "When they closed her trattoria, I was twelve. I promised myself that when I grew up I would make sure it never happened to anyone again. Then I grew up, and I started working for the people who made it happen."

Graziella took the menu and read it carefully, the way you read a letter. Ribollita, pappa al pomodoro, Florentine tripe, cantucci and vin santo. The same dishes, almost in the same handwriting. "Your grandmother had good taste," she said at last. Then she looked up. "And what will you do now?" Valeria Conti smiled for the first time. "Now I'm a consultant. And my first client, if you like, is the City of Florence. Councillor Neri has asked me to help her with the register of historic shops."

Page five, Friday 8 May. Kicker: "Dramatic twist in the Via Maggio affair". Headline: "Ex-manager switches sides". Standfirst: "Valeria Conti, formerly in charge at Arno Living, will work for the city on the register of historic shops. 'I know their numbers better than they do'". Mancini had titled his comment, on the same page, with a single word: "Turning point". Pietro underlined it twice in red pen.

What happened in the following two weeks Pietro understood only in part, even though Valeria explained it to him patiently one evening with a sheet of paper and a pencil. The trattoria had officially entered the register of historic shops. Consequently, the premises could no longer change their business: no sushi bar, no souvenir shop. Moreover, Valeria had shown Arno Living a study with precise figures: in buildings with a historic shop on the ground floor, flats were worth more, not less. "Tourists," she had written, "don't come to Florence to sleep. They come to eat ribollita downstairs."

Page six, Thursday 21 May. This time the headline took up half the front page, and Ferri had written it himself. Kicker: "After a month of tug-of-war". Headline: "Via Maggio, agreement signed: the trattoria stays". Standfirst: "Twelve-year lease for the premises. Six of the twelve flats for residents at capped rents. The Popa family's flat stays as it is". And below, in small print: "The headline of this article was written with the help of Pietro, aged 11".

The agreement had been signed in the trattoria, of course, at the table by the window, the one where Aldo sat every day in 1974. On one side was a gentleman from Arno Living who had come from Milan, with a gold pen and a slightly puzzled air. On the other, Graziella, still wearing her apron. In the middle, Councillor Neri and Valeria Conti. Before signing, the gentleman from Milan had politely asked whether it was true that the house ribollita was the best in Florence. Graziella had looked at him over her glasses. "Sign," she had said. "Then taste."

The gentleman from Milan signed. Then he tasted. Then he asked for a second plate, and then, quietly, whether he could have the recipe. "No," replied Graziella, most kindly. "The recipe stays in Via Maggio. Like the trattoria." Everyone laughed, him included. Matei, who had come down with Viola in his arms, took a photo of the table with the gold pen, the contract and the empty plate. The next day Mancini put it next to his article. It was the best photo in the album, and Davide drew nothing around it: "No need," he said. "It's already perfect."

That evening the neighbourhood threw a party. Nobody had organised it: people simply started arriving. The baker brought bread, the fruit seller strawberries, the barman wine, Lorenzo a crate of beer and his official apologies for having defended short-term rentals. "I'll accept them only if you stay to eat," Graziella told him. Signor Franco made a ten-minute speech nobody listened to, because Viola, who had turned two a few days earlier, had discovered that banging her spoon on the pot made everyone laugh.

Around midnight, when the last guests had gone, Pietro opened the album on the kitchen table and leafed through it from the beginning. Six articles, a cartoon, a photo. Graziella sat down beside him with a cup of camomile tea. "Do you know what's missing?" Pietro said to her. "A headline for the whole album." They thought about it together for a long time. Pietro suggested "The ribollita tug-of-war". Graziella suggested "Seventy-two years young". In the end it was Bellini, who was passing to say goodbye, who found the right one.

"Write this," he said, taking the red pen. On the first page of the album, at the top, in capitals, he wrote a kicker: "A Florentine story". And below, larger, the headline: "Happy ending (for now)". Pietro protested: "For now? But it ended well!" Bellini gave him back the pen. "In Florence, happy endings are always for now," he said. "The city changes, people change. That's why you always need someone who looks carefully, and who writes a letter when it's needed."

Pietro thought for a moment, then nodded. Under Bellini's headline he added a standfirst in his neatest handwriting: "Six articles, two hundred residents, a grandmother, a professor, an artist, a repentant manager, a cat in braces. And the best ribollita in Florence, which is saved. Sources: everyone who has eaten it." Graziella read it, finished her camomile and said only: "The cat didn't wear braces. The editor did." "I know," replied Pietro. "But in headlines you can exaggerate a little." Bellini, in the doorway, laughed so loudly that he woke Lupino under the table.
